verses.translation_literal: Of David. A Maskil. Blessed [is the one] lifted of transgression, covered of sin.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David, and a lesson in it. Oh, the blessedness of the one whose rebellion has been lifted off him like a load from a bent back, whose sin has been covered over, and no one sees it any more.
verses.directors_commentary: Open on a single exhale of relief. The word 'blessed' (אַשְׁרֵי) is plural and exclamatory, the same cry that opens Psalm 1: 'Oh, the happinesses of…'. Here the happiness is not wealth or victory but a debt cancelled. The psalm piles three words for wrongdoing, each with its own picture: פֶּשַׁע is rebellion, a breach of a relationship; חֲטָאָה is missing the mark; and in verse 2 עָוֺן is the crookedness, the twisted guilt that sticks to a person. The speaker holds up two images in parallel: sin is lifted (נשא), like a burden carried away, and covered (כסה), like a wound or a debt closed from sight. The KJV 'forgiven' flattens the first: the Hebrew says literally 'lifted', and the audience would picture the load going off a donkey's back. Note also that the KJV counts the title 'A Psalm of David, Maschil' as verse 0 and the beatitude as its verse 1, while the Hebrew folds both into verse 1; from verse 2 the numbers agree. 'Maskil' probably means an instructive or skilful song; the same root returns in verse 8 ('I will instruct you'), so the psalm names its own purpose in its title. Ancient singers in the temple would have taken this as a teaching piece, not a lament, even though it begins from pain.

philological_notes.note: A psalm-heading of uncertain sense, from the root 'to be wise, to give insight'. It may mean an instructive song, a skilful song, or a name for a musical form. The root recurs as אַשְׂכִּילְךָ in verse 8, which makes the 'teaching' reading attractive here.

'Lifted of transgression': a passive participle of נשא 'to lift, carry', in a construct chain 'one whose rebellion is lifted'. The image is of a burden removed, which is the Hebrew idiom for forgiveness (compare Hos 14:3, cited by Metzudat Zion). The form is irregular, as if from a lamed-he verb.

'Covered of sin': a second passive participle that mirrors the first, so verses 1-2 form a short chain of three synonyms for sin and three for its removal. Covering here is God's act, in contrast to the speaker's own covering of his sin in verses 3 and 5.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [is] a man to whom YHWH does not reckon iniquity, and there is no deceit in his spirit.
verses.translation_dramatic: Oh, the blessedness of the one against whom the LORD keeps no account, who has no ledger of his guilt held over him. And in his spirit, nothing false: no crooked corner, no trick, no hidden door.
verses.directors_commentary: The second beatitude moves from the act to the books. 'Reckon' (חשב) is a bookkeeper's word: God does not enter the debt against a man's name. Paul quotes the Greek of this verse in Romans 4:6-8 for the same reason. The KJV 'imputeth' is theological Latin where the Hebrew is plain accounting. Then comes the condition that makes the whole psalm turn: 'no deceit in his spirit'. Rashi and Radak read this as: forgiveness is real only if repentance is not a trick, not 'I will sin and then repent' (Radak cites the Mishnah, Yoma 8:9). The KJV and ASV 'guile' is archaic; modern readers would say 'deceit' or 'fraud', and רְמִיָּה is the word for a slack, treacherous bow in Ps 78:57. Actors should hear the speaker already half-confessing: the only man blessed is the one who is not hiding anything, and in the next verse we see him recall when he was.

philological_notes.note: 'Reckon, account': an accounting term. Ibn Ezra notes it can mean thinking or calculation. God does not 'charge' guilt to a person's account.
'Deceit, treachery'. Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'like מרמה'. It is the same word used of a deceitful bow in Ps 78:57; so the sense is 'unreliable, slack', not merely 'lying'.

verses.translation_literal: When I kept silent, my bones wore out, in my roaring all the day.
verses.translation_dramatic: While I held my tongue, my bones wore thin. I was a wasting thing, and all day long a low roar came out of me, the sound of a beast in pain, and still I said nothing of my sin.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the psalm turns from teaching to testimony, and the speaker stages his own silence. The silence is not peace but concealment: he kept quiet about his sin, and the body spoke instead. The paradox is in the verse itself: he is silent (החרשתי) and roaring (שאגתי) at once. שאגה is the lion's roar (Ps 22:2, Job 3:24), not a polite 'groan', so the KJV 'roaring' is accurate and the ASV 'groaning' softens it. The bones (עצמים) are the whole frame of the self, and בלה is what clothing and old wineskins do: wear out. The KJV 'waxed old' is quaintly accurate, but it hides that the verb is the same one Sarah uses of her aged body (Gen 18:12). Radak and Meiri read כי as 'when', which is the sense the reader needs; STEPBible's 'if' misleads. Rashi supplies the silence: he kept silent from confessing. Do not play this as quiet. Play it as a held breath that leaks out.

philological_notes.note: 'I kept silent' (hiphil of חרש). Rashi specifies what was withheld: confession of his sins.
'In my roaring': the noun is used of a lion's roar and of cries of anguish; Ibn Ezra compares the lion lifting its voice. The contrast with the preceding 'silent' is intended.

verses.translation_literal: For by day and by night your hand was heavy upon me; my moisture was turned [as] in the dry heats of summer. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: For day and night your hand lay heavy on me, a weight I could not shift. The sap went out of me; I was turned to dust and cracked ground, as the land is parched in the burning heart of summer. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'hand' of God here is a pressure, not a caress: Hebrew uses the hand for power and for the blow. Ibn Ezra says plainly 'hand: your blow'. The night-and-day pair gives the length of the torment, so no breath of relief. Then the image shifts to the land. לְשַׁד is the sap or richness of a living thing, the same word as the 'fresh oil' of the manna cakes in Num 11:8; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all connect them. The KJV 'my moisture' is correct but abstract: the speaker is a green plant in August. חַרְבוֹנֵי קַיִץ is a rare plural, 'the dry heats of summer', and a Judean audience knew it intimately: from May to October there is no rain, the wadis are dust and the leaves go brittle. The KJV's 'drought of summer' renders it well; the ASV's 'as with' adds a simile marker the Hebrew lacks, because בְּ here is likely 'as in'. 'Selah' is a marker whose meaning we do not know: a pause, a lifting of the voice, or an instrument's interlude. Do not fill it with words; let the heat sit.

philological_notes.note: 'My moisture, sap, vitality': the same word as לְשַׁד הַשָּׁמֶן 'cakes baked with fresh oil' in Num 11:8. Rashi also records Menahem's different derivation from שדד 'plunder'.
'In the dry heats of summer': a unique plural from the root of 'dry, ruined' (חרב). Metzudat Zion links it to חרב and to the heat of the sun.
A liturgical marker of unknown meaning: a pause, a rise in pitch, or an instrumental break. It appears here at the end of a thought unit.

verses.translation_literal: My sin I make known to you, and my iniquity I did not cover. I said, 'I will confess over my transgressions to YHWH,' and you, you lifted the guilt of my sin. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: My sin I laid open before you; my wrong I did not cloak. I said, I will speak out my rebellions to the LORD, and you, you yourself, took up the weight of my sin and carried it away. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn of the whole psalm: the silence of v. 3–4 breaks. Note what the speaker does not do. In the ancient Near East, wrongdoing was something you hid from a patron or judge; the verb כסה, 'cover', is the same one the opening verses use of sin that God covers (v. 1), so the speaker refuses to cover what only God should cover. Play the three nouns as three weights: חטאת (a missing of the mark), עון (a bent, twisted thing) and פשע (a breaking away, rebellion). Piling them up is a confession that holds nothing back.

The KJV smooths several things. 'Acknowledged' for אוֹדִיעֲךָ is a soft word; the Hebrew is a hiphil of ידע, 'cause you to know', 'make known', as if informing a judge who in fact knows everything (Radak speaks of 'the way of human speech'). 'Forgavest' for נָשָׂאתָ is right in sense but loses the image: נשא is to lift, to pick up and carry off, a burden lifted from the shoulders. The Hebrew also has an emphatic 'and you' (וְאַתָּה) set against the 'I' of the first half, a pivot the English drops. Rashi ties the scene to David's words to Nathan, 'I have sinned', and Nathan's answer that the LORD has passed over his sin (2 Sam 12:13). 'The guilt of my sin' is a genitive chain: Radak and Meiri read it as intensity, as in 'dust of earth' in Dan 12:2.

philological_notes.note: A hiphil of ידה with a double sense: 'to confess' when its object is wrongdoing and the preposition עַל is used, 'to give thanks' when it is God who is praised. Here the context and עֲלֵי פְשָׁעַי fix 'confess', and Ibn Ezra glosses it 'to confess'. Do not confuse it with אוֹדִיעֲךָ earlier in the verse, which comes from ידע.

'You lifted, carried': the verb of forgiveness as removal of a burden. It echoes the 'one whose transgression is lifted' (נְשׂוּי פֶשַׁע) of v. 1, as Ibn Ezra points out in the same commentary. Radak takes the past form as a prophetic past for what is certain to follow the confession.

verses.translation_literal: On account of this let every faithful one pray to you at a time of finding; surely, to a flood of many waters, to him they will not reach.
verses.translation_dramatic: So let every loyal soul pray to you, while you are there to be found. Then when the great waters rise and roar, a flood that sweeps everything away, they will not touch him.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker turns outward: the personal story becomes a lesson for the whole community, and the 'faithful one' (חָסִיד) is anyone bound to God by chesed, loyal love. 'Because of this' (עַל זֹאת) points to the forgiveness just received. The hard phrase is לְעֵת מְצֹא, 'at a time of finding', and the tradition splits: Ibn Ezra reads 'while God may be found' (compare Isa 55:6), while Radak and Metzudat David read 'when the heart is found whole in repentance'. The KJV chooses the first with 'in a time when thou mayest be found'. 'Surely' (רַק) is another crux: it can restrict ('only') or intensify ('surely'), and Metzudat David and Malbim read it with the flood, as in 'only for a flood of waters'. The flood is the great image of Israel's world: the Jordan in spate, the winter wadi that drowns a caravan, the sea as chaos that Canaanite myth gave to Yam. The KJV's 'come nigh unto him' hides that the verb (נגע) is 'reach, touch': they will not even reach him, the water that sweeps a whole country away.

philological_notes.note: 'The faithful one, the loyal': one who lives in covenant loyalty (חֶסֶד). Meiri observes that a penitent is called חסיד after his end.

'At a time of finding': understood either as the time when God may be found (Ibn Ezra, citing Isa 55:6) or when the heart finds itself free for wholehearted return (Radak, Metzudat David). The Hebrew has no object.
'A flood of many waters': a standard image for overwhelming trouble. Ibn Ezra compares it to Ps 18:17 (ימשני ממים רבים); Rashi reads it as the nations who sweep like water.

verses.translation_literal: You [are] a hiding place for me; from distress you will guard me; [with] shouts of escape you will surround me. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are my hiding place. You keep me from the narrow, crushing places. You will ring me round, and the ring is made of shouting, the sound of those who have slipped free. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker now addresses God directly again, and the tone is warm and close. סֵתֶר is a hiding place, a shelter in the rock, the kind a fugitive in the Judean wilderness would know; the root appears at the opening of Ps 91. Hebrew plays with the sound: מִצַּר תִּצְּרֵנִי, 'from distress you guard me', echoes צר 'narrow place, trouble' with נצר 'to guard' in one phrase. The English 'preserve me from trouble' keeps the sense but not the clatter of tz's. The surprise is the last clause. The KJV 'songs of deliverance' makes it a hymn, but רָנֵּי פַלֵּט is 'shouts of escape': the cries of people who got out alive. And סבב 'to surround', the verb of siege, is used here as protection: where an enemy would ring a city, God rings the speaker with the sound of rescue. The same verb returns in verse 10 with 'covenant loyalty' as subject. Rashi reads תְּסוֹבְבֵנִי as a present, 'you have surrounded me always'.

philological_notes.note: 'From distress you guard me': a pun combining צר 'narrowness, distress' with נצר 'to guard, keep'. Rashi glosses תצרני as 'you will keep me'.
'Shouts of escape': רן is a ringing cry (of joy); פלט is 'escape, a rescued remnant'. Rashi reads it as 'a cry of rescue'.

verses.translation_literal: I will make you understand and I will teach you in the way [in] which you will walk; I will counsel, my eye upon you.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will give you insight, and I will point you down the road you must take. I will advise you, with my eye fixed on you, and watch your every step.
verses.directors_commentary: A new voice breaks in without announcement: the Hebrew has no 'says the LORD', and traditional readers split on whether this is God (Targum, Rashi, Malbim) or David teaching (Radak, Metzudat David). Play it as the voice that spoke in the silence, steady and personal, close enough to read your face. The verbs are three kinds of teaching: אַשְׂכִּילְךָ (give insight, the root of 'Maskil' in the title), אוֹרְךָ (point the way, the root of Torah), and אִיעֲצָה (counsel). The KJV 'guide thee with mine eye' is a famous reading, but the Hebrew is grammatically harder: 'I will counsel, my eye upon you'. Rashi reads אִיעֲצָה as 'I will signal by my eye', and the contrast with verse 9 is exactly that: the learner who needs only a glance versus the animal that needs a bit. A glance is how a master instructs a servant (compare Ps 123:2), and a loved person is guided by a look. The ASV 'with mine eye upon thee' is the more faithful sense.

philological_notes.note: 'I will counsel, my eye upon you': either 'I will advise you with my eye on you' (the watching eye) or 'I will advise by a glance'. Rashi takes it as a signal given by the eye (comparing Prov 16:30). Radak instead takes the eye as the speaker's own experience, 'what I saw with my eyes'.
'I will give you insight': hiphil of שכל, the same root as מַשְׂכִּיל in the title, so the title's 'instruction' is fulfilled here.

verses.translation_literal: Do not be like a horse, like a mule, without understanding; with bit and bridle, its trappings, to restrain, not to come near to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not be like the horse, like the mule, that has no understanding in it: a beast whose jaws must be clamped with bit and bridle, so that it will not come at you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. The confessing 'I' of v. 5 becomes a teacher, and the second person plural turns the lesson on the listeners. Play it as a warning given with affection, and with a dry edge: the audience has just heard that the speaker learned the hard way (vv. 3–4). The horse and the mule are the mounts of the powerful, but here they stand for a creature that is moved only by force, from outside. A bit sits in the mouth, a bridle or halter is held in the rider's hand; the point is that the animal obeys the pull, not the word.

The verse is crowded with difficulties, and honest translators split. עֶדְיוֹ is 'its trappings' or 'ornament', as in Rashi (the animal being groomed and decked out), or 'its mouth, its jaws', as Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra's R. Moshe take it, with Ps 103:5 as parallel. The KJV chooses 'mouth', which is defensible. The last phrase בַּל קְרֹב אֵלֶיךָ is the real fork. The KJV ('lest they come near unto thee'), Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri all agree: the animal is restrained so that it does not come near to bite or kick. The ASV ('else they will not come near unto thee') reads it the opposite way, as if without the bridle the animal would not come to you at all. Ibn Ezra also reports a reading where בל is 'far be it', but the first reading is the simplest. Note the KJV's plural 'which have no understanding'; the Hebrew has a single horse and a single mule, with no 'and' between them (Ibn Ezra: 'in the elegant way, without a vav').

philological_notes.note: From the root of 'ornament, finery' (as in 2 Sam 1:24). Rashi reads 'its trappings', the gear put on a groomed animal; Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read 'its mouth', citing Ps 103:5, 'who satisfies your mouth (עדיך) with good'. The literal layer keeps 'its trappings' because that is what the word usually means.

A poetic negative, 'not', used in verse for לא or אַל. With the infinitive קְרֹב it means 'that it not come near'. The traditional commentators (Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra, Meiri) and the KJV take it as a purpose clause, 'so that it not come near to harm you'; the ASV reads it as a result clause, 'else it will not come near'.

verses.translation_literal: Many [are] the pains of the wicked, but the one trusting in YHWH, covenant loyalty will surround him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Many are the pains that wait for the wicked. But the one who leans his whole weight on the LORD, steadfast love will circle him like a wall.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm closes its teaching with a proverb in two balanced halves. The first half is blunt: 'many pains for the wicked'. מַכְאוֹבִים is pain of body or heart. The second is the reversal: the one who trusts in YHWH is not spared pain but is encircled, and the verb is the siege-word סבב from verse 7. The KJV 'mercy' is too thin for חֶסֶד, which is covenant loyalty, the love of a party who has bound himself by oath, and the ASV 'lovingkindness' is closer. Malbim hears the pain and the surrounding as the same thing seen from two sides: to the one who trusts, the very trials are chesed, a fence that keeps him from the road's edge. The verb בטח means to lean the full weight on something, a good ancient test of a bridge or a wall. Both halves are about the same crowd: the 'wicked' are the stubborn animal of verse 9, and 'the trusting' are the one who answers the glance.

philological_notes.note: 'The one who trusts': a participle of בטח, 'to lean on, feel secure', used for a person who puts his whole weight on another.
'Covenant loyalty, steadfast love': the loyalty of a party bound by covenant. The KJV 'mercy' narrows it. Radak sets it as the exact opposite of the 'many pains' that surround the wicked.

verses.translation_literal: Rejoice in YHWH and be glad, O righteous ones, and shout for joy, all upright of heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rejoice in the LORD, and be glad, you righteous; and let your joy ring out, all you whose hearts run straight.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in a crowd. After the lone 'I' of the confession and the warning of v. 9, three plural commands close the song, and the voice opens out into a shout. Play it as release: the weight of vv. 3–4 is gone, and the people addressed are those who 'trust' (v. 10).

The three verbs are close synonyms with different sounds. שִׂמְחוּ is the general word for joy, גִילוּ is a gladness that spins or leaps, and הַרְנִינוּ is a ringing cry, a loud shout. The KJV renders שִׂמְחוּ 'be glad' and גִילוּ 'rejoice', in the same order as the Hebrew, and 'shout for joy' for הַרְנִינוּ; the English is sound, but its two first verbs are so alike that the Hebrew's difference in sound is lost. The verb הַרְנִינוּ also picks up רָנֵּי, 'shouts of', from v. 7, so the 'shouts of deliverance' that surround the speaker there become the shout the whole community is told to give here; Radak notes that the form is causative, so that the righteous are to make others cry out for joy too. 'Upright of heart' is literally 'straight of heart', the opposite of the twisted (עון) of v. 5 and the 'no deceit' of v. 2.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of רנן, 'to ring out, shout for joy'; the same root as רָנֵּי in v. 7. Radak reads the hiphil as causative, 'cause others to shout for joy', in the sense of bringing good news to the upright.
'Straight of heart': a person whose inner life runs without bends. The phrase answers the 'no deceit' (אֵין בְּרוּחוֹ רְמִיָּה) of v. 1 and sets the people of the psalm against the rasha of v. 10.
